Debug build: these numbers are pessimistic

A debug build runs without R8 or a baseline profile and mostly interpreted, so it drops several times more frames than the same code in a release. Judge with devRelease: ./gradlew :app:installDevRelease
Not enough recorded to score yet: the score needs %1$d frames of drawing.
Every measured metric meets its target.

Each bar is a frame from its vsync to the GPU finishing, the solid part its main-thread work, against the budget at 60, 90 and 120 Hz. Red missed its deadline: a janky frame. Amber made it, but its main thread took longer than the budget.
While drawing, for each of the last 60 seconds; a gap is a second with nothing to draw. The line is the display\'s rate.
Every frame recorded, by its main-thread time in milliseconds. The line is one refresh interval: the time the main thread has for each frame.
Java heap and native heap each second; PSS at most every 15 seconds, in a pause in the drawing.

Open Janky frames by screen and start with the worst screen. The usual causes: recomposition on every frame of an animation (read animated values in graphicsLayer, offset or drawBehind lambdas), alpha on a full-screen layer, work on the main thread during a transition, and a first frame that builds a whole screen. Record a trace with the android-profiler skill to see which.

Ordinary frames keep the main thread busy for most of the frame budget, which leaves no room for a slower one. Look for layouts measured twice (intrinsics, nested weights), lists without contentType, and work in composition that belongs in remember or the draw phase.

The slowest frames keep the main thread busy past the frame budget. These are usually first frames: a screen built for the first time, or a list item type seen for the first time. Make sure the baseline profile covers them, keep first frames small, and defer what the first frame does not show.
Frames over 16 ms miss even a 60 Hz budget. Find them in Frame times and record a trace of that moment.
A frame took longer than 700 ms: the app froze. Something blocked the main thread: disk or network on it (check StrictMode below), a large decode, or a lock. Move it to a background dispatcher.
The main thread did more than 50 ms of work for single frames. StrictMode below names disk and network calls; a trace names the rest. Defer what is not needed for the first frame.

Start-up does too much before the first frame. Keep Application.onCreate and the first screen\'s creation free of I/O and of eager singletons, make sure the baseline profile is compiled, and measure with tools/perf/perf.sh coldstart on devRelease.
Re-creating the activity is slow: the first screen does work on creation that it could keep in its ViewModel, or restores more state than it needs.

The app keeps more memory than the 48 MB budget. Look for caches without a bound, images decoded at full size, and screens that hold their data after they close. A heap dump from the profiler shows who owns it.
The garbage collector stopped every thread. That comes from allocating fast: objects created on every frame, in draw lambdas or animation callbacks. Hoist them into remember or a node.
The main thread touched the disk or the network. The examples below name where; move each call to a background dispatcher, or into a repository that already runs there.
This build is not shrunk by R8, which also optimises the code. Release builds are; measure one: devRelease.

ART has not compiled this build with the baseline profile, so its first use of each screen runs interpreted. On a debuggable build it never will; install devRelease. Otherwise run tools/perf/perf.sh, or adb shell cmd package compile -f -m speed-profile, and turn on the baselineprofile feature if the project lacks one.
A debuggable build turns off most of ART\'s compilation, so it is several times slower than the release. Its numbers are pessimistic; measure devRelease.
